title: UDP & QUIC: Notes from the Wire
summary: A dense study-notes carousel on UDP's connectionless semantics, when it beats TCP, and how QUIC rebuilds reliability over it to power HTTP/3 — with handshakes, head-of-line blocking, trade-offs, and common mistakes.

chapters.title: UDP Fundamentals: The Connectionless Datagram
points: UDP = User Datagram Protocol: no connection setup, no handshake, send and forget
Header is only 8 bytes: src port, dst port, length, checksum
Datagram = self-contained message; no sequence numbers, no ACKs, no retransmission
Checksum is optional in IPv4 (0 = skip) but recommended; catches corruption, not loss
No congestion control, no flow control — the app owns pacing
MTU matters: datagrams over ~1472 bytes (Ethernet) may fragment; fragmentation amplifies loss (lose 1 fragment, drop whole packet)
Best-effort delivery: packets can be lost, duplicated, reordered, or arrive at different times
Socket model: one socket can talk to many peers via sendto()/recvfrom(); no accept()/connect() state machine
Zero connection state in the OS/kernel per peer — scales to millions of flows cheaply
UDP is a thin layer over IP: think 'IP plus ports plus checksum', nothing more
Common uses: DNS, DHCP, NTP, VoIP, gaming, QUIC itself
Gotcha: 'UDP is unreliable' is fine only if the app tolerates loss or rebuilds reliability itself (like QUIC)

chapters.title: When UDP Beats TCP — and When It Doesn't
points: Latency-sensitive real-time: VoIP/video prefer a fresh late sample over a retransmitted old one
Request/response one-shots (DNS): a full TCP handshake triples round trips vs one UDP datagram
Pub/sub and multicast/broadcast: TCP is strictly point-to-point; UDP fans out natively
Live event streams (gaming state, telemetry): latest-wins semantics beat ordered delivery
Firewall/NAT traversal: UDP hole punching is easier and cheaper than TCP simultaneous open
Custom protocol stacks: QUIC, WebRTC RTP, WireGuard all build on UDP to dodge OS TCP constraints
Rule of thumb: use UDP when loss is recoverable OR freshness beats completeness
When NOT UDP: file transfer, web pages, anything needing every byte — loss recovery is hard to do right
When NOT UDP #2: sending large blobs as raw datagrams — fragmentation turns one lost fragment into whole-packet loss
Unmanaged UDP floods can starve links (no congestion control = bad internet citizen)
Middlebox hazard: some networks rate-limit or block UDP entirely; fallback path needed
Middle ground: app-layer reliability over UDP is a big engineering lift — prefer QUIC before hand-rolling

chapters.title: QUIC: Reliability Rebuilt on UDP
points: QUIC (RFC 9000): a secure, multiplexed transport over UDP, origin at Google, standardized by IETF
Design premise: TCP is frozen in kernel + middleboxes; evolve transport in user space over UDP
Encryption is not optional: TLS 1.3 is baked into the protocol — no plaintext QUIC
Most header fields are encrypted; middleboxes can't see or mangle sequence numbers (fixes ossification)
Streams: QUIC multiplexes multiple independent byte streams over one connection
Loss in stream A does not stall stream B — this is the core head-of-line blocking fix
Connection IDs: connection survives IP changes (phone Wi-Fi → LTE) with no re-handshake
Streams are ordered and reliable individually; datagram mode (RFC 9221) offers unreliable delivery too
Every QUIC packet is independently acknowledged — no TCP-style byte-stream ACK dependency
Congestion control pluggable in user space (NewReno default; CUBIC, BBR deployable without OS updates)
Cost: user-space crypto + packet processing uses more CPU than kernel TCP
Adoption: all major browsers + CDNs speak HTTP/3 over QUIC; ~30% of web traffic and growing

chapters.title: The QUIC Handshake: TLS 1.3 Inside
points: Crypto and transport handshake merged: 1-RTT gets you an encrypted, established connection
Compare TCP: handshake (1 RTT) + TLS 1.3 (1 RTT) = 2-RTT before first byte of app data
0-RTT resumption: returning clients send app data in the very first flight — but it's replayable, never use for non-idempotent requests
Initial packets use keys derived from a well-known salt + DCID — Obfuscated, not secret; version negotiation rides along
Handshake flight 1: client → Initial (ClientHello); flight 2: server → Initial + Handshake (ServerHello, cert, Finished)
Flight 3: client sends Handshake Finished + can already carry 1-RTT app data
Transport parameters (max data, idle timeout, flow control windows) travel inside the TLS extension — inseparable from auth
No cleartext stage at all: TCP's options (MSS, window scale) were visible/attackable; QUIC's are encrypted
Address validation: server may require Retry token before spending resources (anti-amplification, anti-spoofing)
Amplification rule: server may send ≤3× bytes received until the client's address is validated
Connection migration = just start sending from a new IP; same Connection ID, no handshake
Gotcha: 0-RTT data can be dropped if server rejects it — app must handle retransmission of the early flight

chapters.title: Killing Head-of-Line Blocking
points: TCP HOL: one lost segment stalls delivery of ALL later data until retransmission arrives — for the whole connection
HTTP/2 over TCP multiplexes streams but inherits TCP's single ordered byte stream → one loss blocks every stream
Loss probability rises with RTT×bandwidth (window size); on 1% loss paths, HOL dominates HTTP/2 performance
QUIC fix: per-stream ordering; receiver reassembles each stream independently, delivers streams that are complete
Loss on stream 2 → streams 1, 3, 4 still delivered immediately to the app
Remaining HOL: the QUIC packet itself — one lost packet carries frames from multiple streams, so ALL those streams lose that data
Mitigation: senders coalesce frames from the same stream per packet when possible
Flow-control HOL: connection-level flow control window can stall all streams if one stream hogs it — sized carefully
Cross-layer caveat: QUIC removes transport HOL, but app-level (HTTP/3 request) dependencies still serialize by choice
Measured effect: biggest wins on lossy/high-RTT networks (mobile, satellite); small gains on clean fiber
Diagram idea: TCP timeline (loss → stall everything) vs QUIC timeline (loss → stall one stream)
Exam trap: 'QUIC eliminates HOL' is only true across streams, not within one stream — a single stream is still ordered/reliable

chapters.title: HTTP/3: The Web over QUIC
points: HTTP/3 = HTTP semantics (RFC 9110) over QUIC instead of TCP — same methods, headers, status codes
Header compression: QPACK (HPACK redesigned) because QUIC streams can arrive out of order
QPACK uses separate encoder/decoder streams + indexed field sections; static table covers common headers
Blocking risk: a compressed header depending on a not-yet-received reference stalls — senders track 'known received count' before using dynamic refs
Request/response mapping: each HTTP request is one QUIC stream; priorities via extensible priority fields
Server push exists but is deprecated in practice; early hints via 103 preferred
Version negotiation is built in: ALPN 'h3' during the TLS handshake (no h2c-style upgrade dance)
Migration means downloads/streams survive network handoffs — a browser-visible UX win
Deployment: served over Alt-Svc or HTTPS DNS records advertising h3; browsers race TCP+TLS vs QUIC on first visit
HTTP/2 fallback mandatory in practice: UDP-blocked networks (some enterprise/captive portals) still common
Same-origin rules, cookies, CORS unchanged — the web's application layer didn't move, only the transport did
Practical win: 0-RTT + no TCP HOL ≈ faster page loads especially on mobile; biggest on repeat visits

chapters.title: QUIC vs TCP+TLS: The Trade-off Table
points: Handshake latency: QUIC 1-RTT (0-RTT on resume) vs TCP+TLS 2-3 RTT
HOL blocking: QUIC per-stream vs TCP whole-connection
Encryption: QUIC mandatory TLS 1.3 vs TCP optional/stacked
Header visibility: QUIC encrypted (no middlebox meddling) vs TCP cleartext (NATs, ossified options)
Mobility: QUIC connection IDs survive IP change vs TCP dies on IP change
CPU cost: QUIC higher (user-space crypto, per-packet processing) vs kernel-optimized TCP
Middlebox compatibility: QUIC can be UDP-blocked/rate-limited vs TCP nearly universally allowed
Evolution: QUIC upgrades ship with app vs TCP upgrades wait for OS/kernel years
Congestion control: QUIC pluggable per-app vs TCP whatever the kernel ships
Debugging: QUIC traffic opaque to tcpdump/wireshark unless you decrypt keys (SSLKEYLOGFILE works for QUIC in modern tools)
Buffer/MTU: QUIC must do PMTUD itself; overhead ~ QUIC header + TLS records per packet vs lean TCP
Verdict: QUIC wins on latency-sensitive, mobile, lossy paths; TCP still wins on raw CPU-bound bulk transfer

chapters.title: Practical Usage & Common Mistakes
points: Never assume UDP delivery for anything that must arrive — add ACK/retry or switch to QUIC/TCP
Mistake: relying on UDP checksum as integrity proof — it's weak (16-bit); app-level hashes for data that matters
Mistake: sending datagrams near MTU — keep app payloads under ~1200 bytes for QUIC, ~512 for safe cross-network UDP (DNS rule)
Mistake: assuming UDP socket buffers are big enough — tune SO_RCVBUF/SO_SNDBUF for high-throughput; silent drops at the kernel are common
QUIC servers: implement Retry + address validation or become a DDoS amplification vector
Mistake: using 0-RTT for POST/payments — replay attacks; restrict to idempotent reads
Mistake: ignoring PMTUD — hardcoding 1500-byte QUIC packets blackholes on paths with tunnels (VPN adds overhead)
Testing: loss/reorder emulation (tc netem, toxiproxy) before shipping a UDP or QUIC app
Observability: expose QUIC metrics (handshake RTT, 0-RTT rate, loss rate, stream resets) — encrypted transport hides them from middleboxes
Client strategy: advertise h3 via Alt-Svc, race against h2, remember the winner — this is how all browsers do it
Firewall/ops note: open UDP 443; verify no deep-packet-inspection box is throttling it
Rule: choose unreliable delivery (QUIC datagrams) only when the next sample supersedes the lost one

chapters.title: Closing Summary: The Decision Map
points: UDP = ports + checksum + nothing: you own reliability, ordering, congestion, security
TCP = reliable ordered stream: right default for bulk and web, but HOL-bound and frozen in kernels
QUIC = the synthesis: UDP's deployability + TCP's reliability + TLS 1.3's security, in user space
Decision: freshness-over-completeness (VoIP, games, telemetry) → raw UDP; everything must arrive → TCP or QUIC
Decision: web delivery, mobile clients, lossy networks → HTTP/3 over QUIC; keep h2 fallback
Three wins to remember: 1-RTT handshake, per-stream HOL elimination, connection migration
One cost to remember: CPU overhead and UDP middlebox hostility — always have a TCP fallback
Mental model: TCP froze transport evolution; QUIC moved it into the app layer where it can iterate
The one-line exam answer: QUIC is what you get when you rebuild TCP's best parts on UDP, with TLS 1.3 welded in
HOL answer refined: eliminated across streams, never within one stream
Deployment reality: encrypted transport shifts visibility from network operators to endpoints — plan your metrics
Next reading: RFC 9000 (QUIC), RFC 9001 (TLS mapping), RFC 9114 (HTTP/3), RFC 9221 (datagrams)
